results.summary: SPELL is a hardware implementation of a minimal stack-based programming language created for The Skull CTF. It executes programs from 256 bytes of volatile program memory, with a 32-byte stack and 32 bytes of data memory, and provides a serial shift-register interface to load programs and inspect internal registers. The design can drive a 7-segment display via its output pins, and silicon tests show it running a demo program that spells "SPELL" at clock speeds up to 156 MHz. Notable features include the use of DFFRAM memory and successful overclocking well beyond the nominal 10 MHz.

This design displays the current time on a VGA monitor, using a pre-generated font stored in registers and 6-bit color to minimize register usage. The time can be adjusted using three input pins for hours, minutes, and seconds, and a fourth input selects between two types of VGA PMOD hardware. It requires an external VGA PMOD and a 31.5 MHz clock, and the colors cycle every minute. Silicon testing confirms it works correctly.

This project generates an animated Perlin noise pattern on a VGA screen, with two selectable patterns controlled by an input pin. The Perlin noise code was created with the help of the Tiny Tapeout AI Assist GPT. It requires a TinyVGA PMOD and a 31.5 MHz clock, and silicon testing confirms it produces a valid VGA signal that looks like colored noise, with the pattern selection input changing the shape.

This is a simple Snake game with VGA output, controlled by four directional buttons. It requires a TinyVGA PMOD and a 31.5 MHz clock. Silicon testing shows the game loads and displays correctly, but it runs too fast, giving the player only a split second before the snake crashes into a wall. This speed issue is a notable limitation.

This project implements the classic Pong video game with VGA output at 640x480 resolution and 60 Hz refresh rate. It requires four switches and one button for gameplay, and external splitters to convert the 1-bit VGA color signals to 8-bit. The design uses counters, range checks, and an FSM to implement the VGA protocol. No silicon test report is provided, so its actual hardware behavior is unknown.

This circuit outputs the string "tiny tapeout" to a 7-segment display by scrolling through characters using a modulo-12 counter. It can be clocked automatically or manually via input pins, and requires no external hardware. Silicon testing confirms it works as intended, displaying the scrolling text. The design is a simple Wokwi project intended for demonstration.

This design implements a padlock that requires a 3-bit code to unlock, displaying status on a 7-segment display. The code is set using input pins and entered via a clock button, with a reset pin to lock the device. Silicon testing reveals errors: the saved code inverts on every clock cycle and the third bit is ignored, allowing some invalid codes to be accepted. The author notes that the correct code can be entered twice in succession to unlock.

This is a small game where the player toggles a switch at the correct moment to light up segments and form a '0' on a 7-segment display. It uses a circular buffer of D flip-flops as a selector and D flip-flops for memory, with combinational logic for the display. The design runs at 10 Hz and requires no external hardware. Silicon testing confirms it works well and is fun, though it is recommended to use the input as a switch rather than a button.

This is a basic first test design that uses a pair of inverters and a pair of AND gates to detect a secret code on three input pins. When the correct code is entered via DIP switches, the display shows the letter 'L'. It requires no external hardware and is intended as a learning exercise for the Tiny Tapeout process. Silicon testing confirms that setting the inputs to the secret code displays an 'L'.

This circuit acts as a configurable timer that counts down from a value set on its inputs (0 to 7) and displays the remaining time in binary form on LEDs. The start input loads the value and begins counting; when the count reaches zero, an end flag is raised. It requires switches for inputs, a button for start, and LEDs for outputs. No silicon test report is provided, so its hardware behavior is not confirmed.
